Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author)
It was my pleasure to review the enclosed manuscript titled “"Physiological Sources of Essential Lipids for Mycoplasma pneumoniae via Protein P116: Innovative Biotechnological Tools for Targeting Atherosclerotic and Hepatic Lesions.” This study investigates the role of the Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MPN) protein P116 in lipid uptake, particularly its ability to extract essential lipids from human lipoproteins (LDL and HDL) and host cells. The authors demonstrate that P116 facilitates MPN survival by acquiring cholesterol, phosphatidylcholine, and sphingomyelin, which are crucial for its membrane structure. The study also explores the interaction of MPN with atherosclerotic plaques and the liver, highlighting the potential of monoclonal antibodies targeting P116 to inhibit cholesterol uptake and bacterial localization. The findings provide insights into MPN pathophysiology and open avenues for developing therapeutic interventions against MPN infections and related cardiovascular complications. The manuscript presents a compelling study on P116-mediated lipid acquisition and its implications for MPN pathogenesis. With additional discussion of lipid metabolism, mechanistic details of P116 function, and therapeutic relevance, the manuscript will be significantly strengthened.
We sincerely appreciate Reviewer’s insightful suggestions, particularly regarding lipid metabolism, P116’s mechanism of action, and translational implications. In response, we have substantially revised the manuscript to deepen the discussion on Mycoplasma lipidomics, incorporating both historical and recent literature to contextualize P116’s role in selective lipid uptake and membrane adaptation, including potential temperature-dependent remodeling. We have clarified the mechanism of lipid acquisition by P116, presenting new data that support a passive, transporter-independent uptake model via a hydrophobic cavity, and highlighted enrichment patterns consistent with MPN’s membrane needs. We have also expanded on MPN’s tropism for lipid-rich tissues and discussed the therapeutic potential of anti-P116 monoclonal antibodies, outlining their limitations and future directions in prophylactic or adjunctive settings.
Comments
1. Discussion of Mycoplasma Lipids and Membranes: The manuscript focuses on lipid acquisition but provides limited discussion on the lipid composition of Mycoplasma membranes. Expanding on how Mycoplasma membranes differ from other bacterial membranes, particularly in their reliance on cholesterol, would provide better context. The authors could also discuss the functional significance of phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin in Mycoplasma membranes and whether their uptake by P116 aligns with known Mycoplasma lipidomics.
In response to the reviewer’s comment, we have expanded the Discussion to better contextualize P116-mediated lipid uptake within the known lipid profile of Mycoplasma pneumoniae membranes, which are markedly different from those of most other bacteria. Unlike typical bacteria, which synthesize their own phospholipids, Mycoplasma species rely almost entirely on the host for exogenous lipids—particularly cholesterol, phosphatidylcholine (PC), and sphingomyelin (SM) (J. Bacteriol. 1970;102:306–310. doi:10.1128/jb.102.2.306-310.1970; Biochim. Biophys. Acta. 1980;604:65–90. doi:10.1016/0005-2736(80)90585-4; J. Bacteriol. 1986;167:299–304. doi:10.1128/JB.167.1.299-304.1986; Science. 2009;326:1263–1268. doi:10.1126/science.1177263). Cholesterol can constitute 30–50% of Mycoplasma membrane lipids—far higher than in most bacteria—where it plays a critical role in stabilizing and rigidifying the membrane (Biochim. Biophys. Acta. 1980;604:65–90. doi:10.1016/0005-2736(80)90585-4). PC helps maintain membrane fluidity, while SM contributes to lipid raft formation, potentially facilitating host–pathogen interactions (Biochim. Biophys. Acta. 1980;604:65–90. doi:10.1016/0005-2736(80)90585-4; J. Bacteriol. 1986;167:299–304. doi:10.1128/JB.167.1.299-304.1986; J. Lipids. 2012;2012:640762. doi:10.1155/2012/640762).
These characteristics align closely with our lipidomic findings, which show that P116 can acquire not only cholesterol but also PC and SM. The revised Discussion (page 14) now explicitly links these uptake patterns to the established Mycoplasma lipid dependency, reinforcing the concept that P116 functions as a lipid scavenger that supports the organism’s unique membrane composition (npj Syst. Biol. Appl. 2020;6:33. doi:10.1038/s41540-020-00153-7).
In general the discussion of lipids, and in particular mycoplasma lipids is rather thin. There have been a number of papers on mycoplasma lipidomes and membranes in the past few years that are not discussed and should be to connect this study with the state-of-the-art. Also a large body of literature from the 1960s-80s, that could provide some useful basis for discussion. Given what is known about Mycoplasma membrane adaptation and lipidome remodeling, it would be interesting for the authors to discuss how P116 could support selective lipid uptake in response to temperature adaptation, for example?
We fully agree that situating our findings within the broader context of Mycoplasma membrane biology strengthens the manuscript. In response, we have substantially expanded the Discussion to incorporate both foundational studies and recent lipidomic analyses (page 14).
Historical studies established that Mycoplasma species maintain membrane homeostasis almost exclusively through uptake of exogenous lipids, especially cholesterol and saturated phospholipids, by modulating the cholesterol-to-phospholipid ratio and the degree of lipid saturation (Microbiol Rev. 1978 Jun;42(2):414–470. doi: 10.1128/mr.42.2.414-470.1978 and Bio-chim Biophys Acta. 1976 Mar 5;426(2):258-70. doi: 10.1016/0005-2736(76)90336-9 J Bacteriol. 1981 Jun;146(3):1124-34. doi: 10.1128/jb.146.3.1124-1134.1981 Membrane Fluidity. Biomembranes, 1984 vol 12. Springer, Boston, MA. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4684-4667-8_7). Recent high-resolution lipidomics has confirmed the remarkable plasticity of these membranes, showing that lipid composition can shift dynamically in response to environmental stressors such as temperature changes (Cell Rep . 2024 Jul 23;43(7):114435. doi: 10.1016/j.celrep.2024.114435). These findings are consistent with lipidomic profiles reported for M. pneumoniae (npj Syst Biol Appl 6, 33 (2020). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41540-020-00153-7).
In light of this, we now discuss how P116 could contribute to such adaptive remodeling. Its broad lipid-binding capacity and selective uptake of key membrane lipids suggest that P116 may act as a molecular gatekeeper, enabling M. pneumoniae to fine-tune its lipidome in response to temperature shifts or other physiological stresses. While direct evidence for temperature-dependent lipid selectivity remains to be established, our results provide a conceptual framework for future studies exploring this mechanism.
2. Mechanism of Lipid Uptake: The study suggests that P116 is essential for lipid acquisition, but the exact molecular mechanism remains unclear. Are there structural analogies between P116 and other lipid transporters? Additional discussion on whether P116 functions as a passive lipid-binding protein or actively mediates lipid transfer would provide some clues about mechanism. Is there any evidence for selective uptake when comparing the lipid composition of the serum vs. the lipids taken up in the experiments? This would be interesting to discuss as well.
We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments regarding the molecular mechanism of lipid uptake by P116. In our previous study (Nature Structural & Molecular Biology, 2023), we determined the structure of P116 using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy and identified a unique architecture featuring a previously uncharacterized fold. This structure revealed a large, solvent-accessible hydrophobic cavity, consistent with a role in lipid binding and capable of accommodating multiple lipid molecules. However, structural comparisons using the DALI server did not reveal any significant analogies between P116 and other experimentally determined protein structures in the Protein Data Bank, including known lipid transporters or carrier proteins.
To further explore its mechanism, we have now performed new lipid uptake assays using CHO cells overexpressing SR-BI, H1299 pulmonary epithelial cells, and J774 macrophages (see restructured Figure 2). P116-mediated cholesterol uptake was unaffected by SR-BI activity, indicating that it does not rely on this pathway.
Furthermore, while the activation of the cholesterol efflux transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1 promotes cholesterol efflux to classical acceptors such as HDL or lipid-free apoA-I, our data show that upregulation of ABCA1 and ABCG1 did not enhance cholesterol transfer to P116. This suggests that, unlike classical acceptors, P116 does not benefit from transporter-mediated efflux. We also investigated whether P116 binds directly to lipoproteins. Incubation with HDL or LDL followed by analysis of the P116 fraction via immunoturbidimetric assays for apoA-I and apoB revealed no evidence of stable binding. Additionally, inhibition of lipase activity using orlistat does not impair P116-mediated lipid uptake, excluding a lipase-dependent mechanism (Supplementary Figure 3). These findings support a model in which P116 mediates lipid acquisition through a passive, diffusion-driven process. Its hydrophobic cavity enables direct extraction of lipids from the environment, without requiring stable interactions with carrier proteins.
Lipidomic analyses reveal that P116 facilitates the uptake of a broad range of host-derived lipids, yet there is a notable enrichment of phosphatidylcholine, sphingomyelin, and cholesterol—three key lipid classes known to be essential for Mycoplasma pneumoniae membrane integrity and function. While this enrichment suggests a degree of compatibility with the organism’s membrane requirements, P116 does not exhibit strict selectivity for these lipids, as it also mediates the uptake of other lipid species. The mechanisms underlying this preferential accumulation remain to be elucidated.
We have now added the new findings, along with updated lipidomic comparisons and a more detailed discussion of potential mechanistic models, in the revised manuscript (Discussion section, second paragraph on page 13, and revised Figures 1 and 2 and supplementary Figures 2 and 3). These additions provide a more comprehensive understanding of P116’s function as a novel lipid acquisition system.
3. Relevance to Atherosclerosis and Liver Localization: The study suggests that MPN preferentially localizes in lipid-rich environments, but a more detailed discussion of the underlying physiological basis (e.g., lipid metabolism in these tissues) would strengthen the discussion.
We agree that elaborating on the physiological basis of MPN localization enhances the interpretation of our findings. Our data indicate that MPN preferentially localizes to lipid-rich tissues, specifically the liver and atherosclerotic plaques, likely driven by the local availability of lipids. Using SPECT/CT imaging, we observed that MPN chassis accumulated specifically in atherosclerotic lesions in LDLR-deficient mice fed a high-fat diet, but not in wild-type mice, indicating that the presence of lesions—characterized by lipid accumulation and altered endothelial integrity—is required for vascular association. In contrast, the liver consistently showed MPN accumulation in both mouse models, which is consistent with its central role in lipid and cholesterol metabolism. Interestingly, although LDLR-deficient livers were larger and richer in lipids, the MPN signal per gram of tissue was lower than in wild-type mice; however, total MPN levels across the whole liver were similar (see restructured Figure 5). These observations suggest a distribution proportional to organ size. It should be noted that hepatic lipid content is elevated in both mouse models, which may facilitate the lipid-tropism of MPN by providing an excess lipid environment regardless of LDLR status. Since the 6-hour post-injection time point used precedes any potential replication, we interpret this as initial lipid-driven accumulation rather than proliferation. Indeed, dissemination of bacteria to organs such as the liver and spleen has been demonstrated in mice orally administered Salmonella enterica serotype Typhimurium (EMBO Rep. 2025 Feb;26(3):656-689. doi: 10.1038/s44319-024-00328-x. Notably, Salmonella reroutes host lysosomal cholesterol via peroxisomes as a bridge, and free cholesterol is essential for the integrity of Salmonella-containing vacuoles and for bacterial proliferation.
We have expanded the Results and Discussion sections (restructured Figure 5 and last paragraph on page 15 and first paragraph on page 16) to include this mechanistic interpretation and to better contextualize MPN localization within tissue lipid metabolism and structure.
4. Monoclonal Antibody Therapeutics: The data indicate that monoclonal antibodies targeting P116 reduce lipid uptake and bacterial colonization. However, it is unclear whether these antibodies could serve as viable therapeutic agents in vivo. Could they be used prophylactically or as adjuncts to antibiotics? It would be interesting to compare the inhibitory effects of these antibodies with other known antimicrobial strategies targeting Mycoplasma.
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment regarding the translational potential of monoclonal antibodies targeting P116. Currently, treatment options for MPN infections are limited. The organism lacks a cell wall, rendering β-lactam antibiotics ineffective, and macrolide resistance is an increasing concern globally. As such, there is an unmet need for novel therapeutic strategies targeting essential bacterial processes. P116 is essential for MPN survival due to its role in lipid acquisition, and our results support its candidacy as a target for intervention. In our study, we evaluated the 3G9 monoclonal antibody against P116 in LDLR-deficient mice using SPECT/CT imaging. Interestingly, despite antibody administration, MPN cells were still detected in the liver up to 6 hours after injection. This contrasts with our ex vivo findings, where 3G9 effectively inhibited the growth of MPN within human atherosclerotic arteries. These results suggest that in vivo dynamics are substantially more complex than ex vivo conditions, likely due to factors such as tissue-specific lipid availability, systemic distribution, or immune compartmentalization, which may influence the accessibility or efficacy of antibody targeting. While our data validate P116 as a potentially druggable target, they also highlight the need for further studies to optimize antibody-based approaches. This includes evaluating pharmacokinetics, in vivo biodistribution, delivery platforms, and combination therapies with existing antibiotics. In particular, prophylactic or adjunctive use of anti-P116 antibodies may offer synergistic benefits in settings of antibiotic resistance or immune compromise.
We now include this clarification and discussion (second paragraph on page 16) in the revised manuscript to better frame the limitations and future directions for P116-based interventions.
5. The study relies on in vitro assays and ex vivo tissue models. Additional discussion on how these findings might translate to in vivo infection models or clinical scenarios is warranted.
To address the clinical relevance of our findings, we have expanded the Discussion to emphasize their implications at three different levels:
- Therapeutic targeting and vaccine development: P116 is essential for MPN viability, and antibodies raised against its C-terminal domain exhibit strong growth-inhibitory effects in vitro. This suggests that P116, particularly its C-terminal region, could be a promising candidate for vaccine development or targeted immunotherapy.
- Extrapulmonary manifestations of MPN: While MPN is primarily associated with respiratory infections, it has also been implicated in extrapulmonary pathologies, including liver involvement. Reports have described elevated liver enzymes, and in rare cases, acute hepatitis or cholestasis—especially in pediatric patients (Microb Pathog 2020 Feb:139:103863. doi: 10.1016/j.micpath.2019.103863). Our findings offer a possible mechanistic explanation for these clinical observations. The P116-mediated lipid scavenging mechanism may drive MPN accumulation in lipid-rich tissues such as the liver and atherosclerotic plaques. While our current ex vivo models support tissue-specific localization based on lipid content, we agree that additional in vivo studies are essential to confirm the role of P116 in organ-specific colonization and pathogenesis.
- Biotechnological applications: The MPN chassis is being explored as a delivery platform for therapeutic use in lung diseases. Our discovery that the MPN chassis can also efficiently target the liver and atheromatous plaques opens new possibilities for engineering targeted delivery vehicles to non-pulmonary tissues, expanding its potential in translational biotechnology.
These perspectives have now been incorporated into the revised manuscript to better contextualize the broader significance of our findings and highlight future directions for both research and therapeutic application (pages 15 and 16).
6. Given the importance of lipidomic analyses, a more explicit discussion of the UHPLC-MS workflow and data normalization methods would improve reproducibility. For example, what standards were used to quanitify which lipids, were they added before or after lipid extraction, concentrations, etc…?
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment highlighting the importance of detailed lipidomic methodology to ensure reproducibility. In response, we have expanded the Methods section to include a more explicit description of the UHPLC-MS workflow and data normalization procedures (page 22 and the first paragraph on page 23).
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
This study provides new insights into the role of the P116 protein in M. pneumoniae lipid uptake and its potential impact on bacterial survival in the bloodstream. The authors present compelling evidence that P116 helps extract essential lipids from LDL and HDL, a key adaptation for M. pneumoniae in lipid-rich environments. These findings are particularly important as they link M. pneumoniae colonization in liver and atherosclerotic lesions to its ability to acquire essential lipids. To further improve the study’s impact and reproducibility, consider addressing the following points:
We thank the reviewer for their positive assessment and valuable suggestions. In response, we have strengthened the study by increasing biological replicates and applying more rigorous statistical analyses to enhance reproducibility. We have incorporated new quantitative measurements of MPN chassis accumulation in liver and atherosclerotic tissues using both imaging and qPCR, establishing correlations with tissue lipid content and lesion severity. Additional mechanistic insights were gained from lipid uptake assays in multiple cell types, clarifying that P116 mediates lipid acquisition via a passive, diffusion-driven process. These comprehensive updates deepen our understanding of P116’s role in MPN survival and its localization in lipid-rich tissues, thereby improving the study’s overall impact.
In Figures 1 and 2, where human circulating LDLs and HDLs are identified as primary lipid sources for P116, including at least three replicates would strengthen statistical robustness and reproducibility.
We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we have increased the number of biological replicates to at least n=3 for all lipidomic analyses, including those previously shown in Figures 1D and 2B (now included into the updated Figures 1 and 2d, and supplementary data). To ensure appropriate statistical analysis, we replaced multiple t-tests with one-way ANOVA for both overall group comparisons and individual lipid species. Additionally, we now report standard deviations (SDs) instead of standard errors of the mean (SEMs) to more accurately represent variability within small sample sizes. The inclusion of additional replicates and new experiments did not change the outcomes of our original findings.
The same applies to Figure 3C on lipid uptake. Testing the mAb-3B5 antibody (which does not target the central region of P116) would further confirm that only antibodies targeting the C-terminal domain interfere with lipid acquisition and M. pneumoniae presence in atherosclerotic tissue.
In response, we have performed additional experiments to directly assess the ability of mAb-3G9 to inhibit cholesterol transfer from LDL to P116, comparing the results with those obtained using the antibody mAb-3B5. As shown in the revised Figure 3c, only mAb-3G9 significantly reduced cholesterol transfer to P116, whereas mAb-3B5 had no effect. These findings confirm that inhibition of lipid acquisition is specific to antibodies targeting the C-terminal domain of P116.
Since M. pneumoniae lacks traditional energy-dependent lipid transporters, diffusion is likely the mechanism by which P116 mediates cholesterol and neutral lipid uptake. Investigating whether cellular transporters contribute to this process would provide valuable mechanistic insights into P116’s function.
To further investigate whether host cellular transporters contribute to the lipid acquisition mechanism of P116, we have performed new cholesterol uptake assays using CHO cells overexpressing SR-BI, H1299 pulmonary epithelial cells, and J774 macrophages. Our results show that P116-mediated cholesterol uptake is unaffected by SR-BI expression or activity, indicating that P116 does not rely on this receptor-mediated pathway (new restructured Figure 2b). Furthermore, while the activation of the cholesterol efflux transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1 promotes cholesterol efflux to classical acceptors such as HDL or lipid-free apoA-I, our data show that upregulation of ABCA1 and ABCG1 did not enhance cholesterol transfer to P116 (new Figure 2c). This suggests that, unlike classical acceptors, P116 does not benefit from transporter-mediated efflux. These findings support a model in which P116 functions as a passive lipid-binding protein, directly capturing cholesterol and other essential lipids from LDL, HDL and host membranes.
Other points:
In Figures 4 and 5, including quantitative measurements of signal intensities would provide an objective assessment of the observed visual changes.
Establishing a numerical correlation between liver lipid content and M. pneumoniae presence would further validate the physiological impact of P116-mediated lipid uptake.
We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. In response, we have performed quantitative analyses to objectively assess the observed visual changes in Figures 4 and 5. For Figure 4 (ex vivo imaging), we have quantified signal intensities corresponding to MPN accumulation in four independent tissues. In the restructured Figure 5, we have quantified liver-associated signals using radioactivity measurements from SPECT/CT imaging, enabling an objective assessment of MPN localization in this organ. In addition, the presence of MPN in livers has been confirmed and quantified by qPCR, which has been included as a complementary measurement to the imaging data.
To address the reviewer’s request for physiological correlation, we analyzed the relationship between MPN abundance and tissue lipid content. Specifically, we correlated radioactivity- and qPCR-based MPN quantification with hepatic cholesterol levels and proximal aortic atherosclerosis. Notably, no significant correlation was found between liver cholesterol content and MPN abundance (Figure 5f). This suggests that while liver accumulation may reflect a general lipid-driven tropism, it does not correlate directly with hepatic lipid levels—likely because MPN is diffusely distributed throughout the liver tissue. The elevated hepatic lipid levels in both mouse models may create a permissive environment that facilitates MPN tropism, independently of LDLR status, particularly at the 6-hour post-injection time point before any bacterial replication occurs. Consistent with this, MPN was detected in atherosclerotic plaques of LDLR-deficient mice fed a high-fat diet, but not in wild-type controls that do not develop significant atherosclerotic lesions, indicating that lesion formation is required for vascular association. This supports our interpretation that P116-mediated lipid acquisition promotes selective MPN localization in lipid-rich, structurally compromised vascular lesions.
These new quantitative data and correlations have been incorporated into the revised Figures 4c and 5f, and are discussed in the updated Results and Discussion sections (pages 10, 11, 15 and 16) to better contextualize the physiological relevance of MPN distribution.
Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript describes a series of experiments designed to substantiate a hypothesis, as written in l609-611, that ‘P116 plays a critical role in extracting essential lipids from physiological circulating lipoproteins and from a diversity of cell types, which can explain the colonization of different tissues by MPN’. Unfortunately, there are several weaknesses in the design and interpretation of the data which limit the conclusions which can be drawn from this work.
We appreciate the careful evaluation of our hypothesis and the detailed critique of our experimental design and data interpretation. In response, we have performed several additional experiments, clarified key mechanistic points, revised overstated conclusions, and improved the overall presentation of the data. These changes have strengthened the rigor of our findings and helped refine our model of P116 as a lipid acquisition factor in MPN. We believe that the revised manuscript more clearly and accurately conveys our conclusions, and we are grateful for the reviewer’s insights, which have significantly improved the quality of the work.
Major points
1. The model for the function of P116 is unclear; the structure suggests it is a lipid-binding protein attached to the mycoplasma membrane by a flexible linker (l69). But is it acting as an adhesin or as part of an uptake system for lipid nutrients- the authors seem to suggest the latter (l62)? However, interpretation of the data in the manuscript does not draw a clear distinction between these two models for the role of P116.
We agree that clearly distinguishing between potential functions of P116 is critical for interpreting its biological relevance. Based on our structural, biochemical, and in vivo data, we favor a model in which P116 primarily functions as part of a lipid acquisition system. P116 is a membrane-anchored protein connected by a flexible linker, as we previously reported (Nature Structural & Molecular Biology, 2023 30, 321–329, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41594-023-00922-y). The structure revealed a unique fold with a large, solvent-accessible hydrophobic cavity, consistent with a lipid-binding role. P116 can bind to lipoproteins and host cell membranes to extract essential lipids from them; however, it is not the main adhesin, as previous studies have shown that the Nap complex (composed of the P1 and P40/P90 proteins) is the primary adhesion mechanism of M. pneumoniae and M. genitalium (Nat Commun 2020 11, 5188, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-18777-y) To further investigate whether host cellular transporters contribute to the lipid acquisition mechanism of P116, we have performed new cholesterol uptake assays using CHO cells overexpressing scavenger receptor type BI (SR-BI), H1299 pulmonary epithelial cells, and J774 macrophages. Our results show that P116-mediated cholesterol uptake is unaffected by SR-BI expression, indicating that P116 does not rely on this receptor-mediated pathway (new restructured Figure 2b). Furthermore, while the activation of the cholesterol efflux transporters ATP-binding cassette (ABC)A1 and ABCG1 promotes cholesterol efflux to classical acceptors such as HDL or lipid-free apoA-I, our data show that upregulation of ABCA1 and ABCG1 did not enhance cholesterol transfer to P116 (new Figure 2c). This suggests that, unlike classical acceptors, P116 does not benefit from transporter-mediated efflux.
This disrupted pattern of cholesterol acquisition when P116’s lipid-binding ability is blocked by antibodies targeting its C-terminal domain (see updated Figure 3) and the lack of stable complexes with lipoproteins, further support its role in nutrient uptake rather than adhesion. Overall, we have not observed evidence of host receptor-dependent binding or adhesion mediated by P116 in any of our previous (Nature Structural & Molecular Biology, 2023) or present assays. Unlike typical adhesins, P116 does not show high-affinity or saturable binding to cellular surfaces. These observations strongly support the idea that P116 functions primarily in lipid scavenging rather than adhesion. We have now clarified this distinction in the revised Discussion section (second paragraph on page 13 and page 14) to better articulate the mechanistic model and distinguish between these two possible functions.
2. The heading for section 3.1 over-states the conclusion which can be drawn from these experiments ‘Human circulating LDL is a major source of unesterified cholesterol for MPN P116’ (l436). All that can be said about the results from Fig 1 is that cholesterol from LDLs or HDLs in vitro binds to P116. This may or may not happen in vivo. It is clear from the results in section 3.2 that the specificity of P116 is broad.
We agree that the original heading may have overstated the relevance of the findings presented in Section 3.1. We have modified the heading to: 'Human LDL is a source of unesterified cholesterol for MPN P116' to better reflect the experimental context and avoid overinterpretation. To support the relevance of these findings, we have conducted additional experiments to assess whether cholesterol is specifically transferred from lipoproteins to MPN (see updated Figure 1b). These results suggest that LDL can serve as a viable cholesterol source under controlled conditions, although we refrain from making in vivo claims at this stage (second paragraph on page 12 and first paragraph on page 13).
The text, section heading, and figure legends have all been revised accordingly to clarify that our conclusions are based on controlled in vitro experiments.
3. The description of the conclusion in section 3.3 implies an active function of P116 in lipid acquisition- ‘P116 uptakes lipids from H1299 lung cells with low efficiency’- which is not necessarily warranted by the data. If P116 is simply a lipid-binding protein, it will presumably bind free cholesterol in solution. Cells with lower cholesterol content and/or less propensity to shed cholesterol will transfer less of it to P116. This is more a property of the cells studied than of P116 itself.
We agree that the original sentence in Section 3.3 may imply a level of active function by P116 that goes beyond what the data directly support. As the reviewer points out, P116 can be described as a high-capacity lipid-binding protein that passively acquires lipids from its environment. Our revised interpretation acknowledges that the efficiency of cholesterol acquisition by P116 in co-culture assays largely reflects the lipid availability of the host cells (see restructured Figure 2). Indeed, the observed differences in cholesterol transfer from H1299 lung cells compared to other cell types are likely due to lower cellular cholesterol content (new supplementary Figure 2).
The structure-function relationship supports a model in which P116 passively captures cholesterol by a mechanism driven by favorable thermodynamics rather than receptor-mediated efflux. We have now revised the relevant section and figure legends to clarify this interpretation and avoid overstating the active role of P116. The revised Discussion emphasizes that P116 functions as a passive lipid scavenger, with the extent of lipid uptake primarily dictated by the properties of the surrounding cells and prevailing lipid gradients (page 13).
4. The data on serum reactivity against different forms of P116 lacked suitable controls from uninfected patients (Supplementary Table 4). Some bacterial antigens exhibit a high degree of reactivity against serum IgG, even in individuals with no history of infection by that organism. At the very least, a statistical comparison is needed between infected and uninfected groups to establish the conclusion proposed. It is a stretch to suggest ‘..C-terminal domain of P116 could serve as a promising candidate for the development of vaccines against MPN’ (l591). What reason is there to think that it will elicit a protective immune response?
Following your recommendation, we have now included a statistical comparison of serum reactivity between MPN-infected and uninfected individuals (Supplementary Figure 4). This analysis shows that sera from uninfected individuals exhibited very low reactivity against all P116 constructs compared with infected patients, confirming the specificity of the immune recognition to MPN infection.
As detailed in the Results, all infected patients tested positive for the P116/30–957 and P116/30–845 constructs, whereas removal of both terminal regions (P116/246–818) resulted in a marked reduction in reactivity. Overall, P116/30–957 and P116/30–845 showed stronger reactivity than P116/246–818 (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Table 1).
In addition, a panel of antibodies against P116 (residues 30–957) was tested, and all except one targeted the core domain and showed inhibitory effects on MPN growth and adhesion. Based on these results, mAb 3G9 was selected for further experiments as it exhibited the strongest inhibitory effect. We also included mAb 3B5, which lacks specificity for the central region and exhibits lower affinity.
We agree with the reviewer that the ability of the C-terminal domain of P116 to elicit a protective immune response remains to be determined. Our data support that this domain is immunogenic and specifically recognized during infection, and that antibodies targeting epitopes in this region (e.g., mAb-3G9) can interfere with P116 function, cholesterol uptake, and MPN growth in vitro (Fig. 3b–d). While these findings suggest that the C-terminal domain may represent a promising candidate for future vaccine or therapeutic development, we have revised the manuscript to present this as a possibility rather than a definitive conclusion (first paragraph on page 15).
5. Fig 3C Is the result from one experiment? Is there a control with an antibody without specificity for P116?
We have performed additional experiments to directly evaluate the ability of mAb-3G9 to inhibit cholesterol transfer from LDL to P116 and compared these results with the effects of non-inhibitory antibody mAb-3B5, which targets a different region of P116. The revised Figure 3c now includes three independent biological replicates and includes mAb-3B5. As shown in the restructured Figure 3c, only mAb-3G9 significantly reduced cholesterol uptake, while mAb-3B5 had no effect. These findings confirm that interference with lipid acquisition is specific to antibodies targeting the C-terminal domain of P116. This additional evidence further supports the functional importance of the C-terminal domain in lipid binding and uptake, and reinforces the specificity of mAb-3G9 as a mechanistic probe.
6. Fig 3D: why would MAb-3G9 inhibit growth? Does this imply that P116 plays a role in lipid nutrient uptake?
As shown in the revised Figure 3, treatment with mAb-3G9 significantly inhibits both cholesterol transfer to P116 and MPN growth. This effect is consistent with mAb-3G9 binding to the C-terminal domain of P116, which appears to modulate the size of its hydrophobic cavity to accommodate lipid cargo (updated Figure 3b). These results support the interpretation that P116 facilitates cholesterol acquisition, and that mAb-3G9 inhibits growth by functionally blocking this essential activity. We have revised the text to clarify this mechanism and its implications for MPN lipid acquisition (last paragraph on page 14 and first paragraph on page 15).
7. The microscopy data in Fig 4B are unclear; limited samples are shown and there is no quantification of fluorescence, which would enable a statistical analysis of the effects of both antibodies. Without that, the conclusions are qualitative at best and appear tenuous.
As requested, we have performed quantitative analysis of the fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4. Specifically, we have quantified fluorescence intensities from four independent biological replicates to assess the effects of mAb-3G9 and mAb-3B5 on MPN adherence to human carotid atherosclerotic plaques. The analysis shows that treatment with mAb-3G9 leads to a significant reduction in fluorescence intensity, consistent with impaired lipid acquisition and reduced MPN viability, while mAb-3B5 has no significant effect. These quantitative results are now included in the revised Figure 4c, with full statistical details provided in the figure legend and described in the Methods section.
8. The interpretation of the [¹¹¹In]In-oxine radiolabelling experiments depends on the in vivo fate of the ¹¹¹In label. [¹¹¹In]In-oxine is a neutral, lipophilic complex which passively diffuses through cell membranes. Inside the cell, the isotope binds to intracellular macromolecules. In the literature, [¹¹¹In]In-oxine has been described as a label for leukocytes but I am not aware of any details about Mycoplasma labelling. The labelling period is only 15 minutes (l402)- how do we know that any labelling of the bacteria has occurred at all? Has the isotope been taken up into the bacteria? Could the results in Figure 5 be explained by the lipophilic nature of the complex, preferentially targeting to the fat-enriched livers of the LDL-knockout mice? More data are needed to exclude these explanations.
Prior to the in vivo imaging studies, we confirmed efficient incorporation of [¹¹¹In]In-oxine into both the CV8 MPN chassis and wild-type MPN cells (WT) via in vitro imaging, demonstrating successful bacterial labeling. Although [¹¹¹In]In-oxine is a neutral, lipophilic complex capable of passive diffusion, we took care to verify that the radiolabel was indeed internalized by the bacteria rather than remaining unbound (figure for reviewer). To address the concern that the liver signal might result from nonspecific accumulation of free tracer due to its lipophilicity, we performed qPCR analyses on liver tissue, which detected significant MPN DNA loads consistent with bacterial presence (new Figure 5e). This confirms that the in vivo signal corresponds to labeled bacteria rather than free or unincorporated isotope. Representative images from the in vitro uptake experiments have now been included for review, and we have expanded the Methods section to detail these validation procedures (the last paragraph on page 31 and the first paragraph on page 32).
